title: Opposite interval mapping object exchanges endpoints
statement:
Use small simplicial sets, degreewise products, internal functor simplicial sets and endpoint evaluations of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. For $\theta:[m]\to[n]$ put $\theta^{\mathrm{rev}}(j)=n-\theta(m-j)$; define $K^{\mathrm{op}}_m=K_m$ with operator $K^{\mathrm{op}}(\theta)=K(\theta^{\mathrm{rev}})$. Put $I=\Delta^1$. For every small simplicial set $E$ the formula
$$R_{E,n}(\alpha)_m(i,\theta)=\alpha_m(i^{\mathrm{rev}},\theta^{\mathrm{rev}}),\qquad \alpha:I\times\Delta^n\to E,$$
where $i:[m]\to[1]$ and $\theta:[m]\to[n]$, defines a natural simplicial isomorphism
$$R_E:\operatorname{Fun}(I,E)^{\mathrm{op}}\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Fun}(I,E^{\mathrm{op}}).$$
It satisfies $\operatorname{ev}_a R_E=(\operatorname{ev}_{1-a})^{\mathrm{op}}$ for $a=0,1$, as maps to $E^{\mathrm{op}}$. For every simplicial map $p:E\to B$ it satisfies $R_B\operatorname{Fun}(I,p)^{\mathrm{op}}=\operatorname{Fun}(I,p^{\mathrm{op}})R_E$. The opposite of a degreewise pullback is the pullback of the opposite maps. Thus these identifications carry the opposite of $\rho_0(p)$ to $\rho_1(p^{\mathrm{op}})$, where
$$\rho_a(p):\operatorname{Fun}(I,E)\to\operatorname{Fun}(I,B)\times_{\operatorname{ev}_a,B}E,\qquad \alpha\mapsto(p\alpha,\alpha(a)).$$
No Kan condition is imposed on $E$ or $B$.

source.place: SSet.op, op_map and the degreewise definition of the simplicial internal hom; explicit reversal formula

proof.text: Write $r_j(t)=j-t$ on the underlying set $[j]$, so $u^{\mathrm{rev}}=r_bur_a$ for $u:[a]\to[b]$. This composite is monotone: $s\leq t$ implies $a-t\leq a-s$, hence $b-u(a-s)\leq b-u(a-t)$. Cancellation of the two intervening reflections gives $(vu)^{\mathrm{rev}}=v^{\mathrm{rev}}u^{\mathrm{rev}}$, $(\mathrm{id})^{\mathrm{rev}}=\mathrm{id}$ and $(u^{\mathrm{rev}})^{\mathrm{rev}}=u$. Therefore the operators specified in the statement define $K^{\mathrm{op}}$, and a simplicial map $f$ has $f^{\mathrm{op}}$ with the same degreewise components; naturality follows from that of $f$ applied to $u^{\mathrm{rev}}$. Applying opposite twice is identity. Here the standard-simplex operators and all map equalities are those of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones].

source.place: SimplexCategory.rev and rev_map_apply, lines 27-45; elementary reflection identities

proof.text:
Fix $\alpha:I\times\Delta^n\to E$ and put $\beta_m(i,\theta)=\alpha_m(i^{\mathrm{rev}},\theta^{\mathrm{rev}})$. For $u:[l]\to[m]$, naturality of $\alpha$ and Step 1 give
$$\begin{aligned}E^{\mathrm{op}}(u)\beta_m(i,\theta)&=E(u^{\mathrm{rev}})\alpha_m(i^{\mathrm{rev}},\theta^{\mathrm{rev}})\\&=\alpha_l(i^{\mathrm{rev}}u^{\mathrm{rev}},\theta^{\mathrm{rev}}u^{\mathrm{rev}})\\&=\alpha_l((iu)^{\mathrm{rev}},(\theta u)^{\mathrm{rev}})=\beta_l(iu,\theta u).\end{aligned}$$
Thus $\beta$ is an actual simplicial map $I\times\Delta^n\to E^{\mathrm{op}}$, not merely a function on vertices. By the internal functor definition in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], it is an $n$-simplex of the required target.

source.place: SSet.op_map, lines 55-58; naturality calculation for the explicit reversal formula

proof.text: For $\sigma:[k]\to[n]$, the operator of $\sigma$ on $\operatorname{Fun}(I,E)^{\mathrm{op}}$ sends $\alpha$ to $\alpha\circ(\mathrm{id}_I\times\Delta(\sigma^{\mathrm{rev}}))$. The operator in the target is restriction by $\mathrm{id}_I\times\Delta(\sigma)$, by [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. On an arbitrary $l$-simplex $(i,\tau)$ with $\tau:[l]\to[k]$, the latter restriction of $R_{E,n}(\alpha)$ has value $\alpha_l(i^{\mathrm{rev}},(\sigma\tau)^{\mathrm{rev}})=\alpha_l(i^{\mathrm{rev}},\sigma^{\mathrm{rev}}\tau^{\mathrm{rev}})$, exactly the value of $R_{E,k}$ on the former restriction. Hence the displayed degreewise maps form a simplicial map $R_E$, for faces and degeneracies alike.

source.place: SSet.op_map; the internal-functor operators in def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones

proof.text: The same formula gives its inverse. More explicitly, for $\beta:I\times\Delta^n\to E^{\mathrm{op}}$ put $S_n(\beta)_m(i,\theta)=\beta_m(i^{\mathrm{rev}},\theta^{\mathrm{rev}})$, viewed in $E_m$. Step 2 applied to $E^{\mathrm{op}}$ and Step 1 show that this is a simplicial map to $E$. Step 3 applied to $E^{\mathrm{op}}$ shows that $R_{E^{\mathrm{op}}}:\operatorname{Fun}(I,E^{\mathrm{op}})^{\mathrm{op}}\to\operatorname{Fun}(I,E)$ is simplicial; taking its opposite gives exactly $S:\operatorname{Fun}(I,E^{\mathrm{op}})\to\operatorname{Fun}(I,E)^{\mathrm{op}}$. For either composite its value at $(i,\theta)$ is obtained by reversing both coordinates twice, so is the original value. Thus $S R_E$ and $R_E S$ are identities, proving the simplicial isomorphism.

source.place: SSet.opFunctorCompOpFunctorIso, lines 88-94; double reversal calculated explicitly

proof.text: Let $c_a:[n]\to[1]$ be constant at $a$. Endpoint evaluation on an $n$-simplex $h:I\times\Delta^n\to E$ is $h_n(c_a,\mathrm{id}_{[n]})$, by restriction to the vertex as in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. Since $c_a^{\mathrm{rev}}=c_{1-a}$ and $\mathrm{id}^{\mathrm{rev}}=\mathrm{id}$, evaluation of $R_{E,n}(\alpha)$ at $a$ is $\alpha_n(c_{1-a},\mathrm{id})$. This is the degree-$n$ value of $(\operatorname{ev}_{1-a})^{\mathrm{op}}$, proving both endpoint identities. For any simplicial map $p:E\to B$, both $R_B\operatorname{Fun}(I,p)^{\mathrm{op}}$ and $\operatorname{Fun}(I,p^{\mathrm{op}})R_E$ take $(\alpha;i,\theta)$ to $p_m\alpha_m(i^{\mathrm{rev}},\theta^{\mathrm{rev}})$. This proves the stated strict naturality in $E$ and the compatibility with every $p$.

source.place: SSet.opFunctor_map, lines 51-53; vertex restriction and postcomposition calculated explicitly

proof.text: For a cospan $A\xrightarrow{f}C\xleftarrow{g}D$, write its degreewise pullback as $P_n=\{(x,y)\in A_n\times D_n:f_n(x)=g_n(y)\}$. The operator for $u:[m]\to[n]$ on $P^{\mathrm{op}}$ sends $(x,y)$ to $(A(u^{\mathrm{rev}})x,D(u^{\mathrm{rev}})y)$, exactly the operator on $A^{\mathrm{op}}\times_{C^{\mathrm{op}}}D^{\mathrm{op}}$. These equalities identify the projections as well. Thus opposite preserves the specified pullback by the identity on pairs. This is a calculation from the degreewise product and pullback conventions of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], with no limit-preservation theorem required.

source.place: SSet.op and op_map; degreewise products in Monoidal.lean, lines 124-127; pullback calculated on pairs

proof.text:
Let $P_a(p)=\operatorname{Fun}(I,B)\times_{\operatorname{ev}_a,B}E$. Steps 5 and 6 define an isomorphism $T:P_0(p)^{\mathrm{op}}\to P_1(p^{\mathrm{op}})$, $T_n(\gamma,e)=(R_{B,n}(\gamma),e)$: its defining equality is $\operatorname{ev}_1R_B(\gamma)=\operatorname{ev}_0(\gamma)=p_n(e)$ in the common degree-$n$ set. The inverse is $(\eta,e)\mapsto(S_{B,n}(\eta),e)$, which satisfies the reverse equality by Step 5. Using the endpoint and naturality equalities of Step 5, for every $\alpha$ one has
$$T_n\rho_0(p)^{\mathrm{op}}_n(\alpha)=(R_{B,n}(p\alpha),\alpha(0))=(p^{\mathrm{op}}R_{E,n}(\alpha),(R_{E,n}\alpha)(1))=\rho_1(p^{\mathrm{op}})_nR_{E,n}(\alpha).$$
This is the asserted identification of the actual corner maps. All constructions use only functions, their equalities and the degreewise conventions of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. They require no horn fillers, no Kan hypothesis and no nonempty sets.
